en: The Sūtra on the Causes of the Aggregate of Suffering Spoken by the Buddha, translated by the Śramaṇa Dharmajva of the Western Jin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śakrāditya, among the Kṣatriya clan of the Vṛṣṇis.
In the city of Rājagṛha, within the Nyagrodha Grove,
the Śākya Mahānāma wandered about in the afternoon and went to where the World-Honored One was.
Upon arrival, he prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One and withdrew to sit to one side.
Having sat down to one side, the great strongman addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“I fully understand the Dharma as taught by the World-Honored One, namely, the three fetters of mental attachment:
the fetter of mental attachment to lust, the fetter of mental attachment to hatred, and the fetter of mental attachment to delusion.”

Thus it is; I fully understand all that the World-Honored One has taught: that my mind is now attached to the dharma of sensual desire, and that my mind is already attached to the dharmas of anger and delusion.
"Therefore, indeed, World-Honored One!
I have had this thought:
'What dharma do I still possess that has not been exhausted, such that it causes lustful desire to arise and my mind to become attached to it?'"
“Do you give rise to states of anger and delusion, and become attached to them in your mind?

“O Great Malla! Since the Dharma has not yet reached its end for you, it does not permit you to remain at home, nor does it require you to train in the Path, nor does it demand that you lose faith in and delight in leaving the household life to renounce the home.”

"O Great Malla! If this Dharma were to come to an end, you too would not remain at home; you would surely be able to find faith and joy in leaving the household life to renounce your home and study the Path. O Great Malla!"
"Because those dharmas have not yet been exhausted, they cause you, while living at home, to lack faith and joy, leading you to leave the household life and study the Way.
Thereupon, the Malla Mahānāma rose from his seat, adjusted his robe over one shoulder, joined his palms toward the World-Honored One, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"Thus, I now have faith and joy in the World-Honored One; I only pray that the World-Honored One [will grant me ordination]!"
"Preaching the Dharma skillfully means seeing the Dharma so that doubt is exhausted.
"O Great Malla! There are five types of sensual desire:
longing for love, longing for beauty, intimacy with sensuality, and attachment."

The eye cognizes forms, the ear cognizes sounds, the nose cognizes odors, the tongue cognizes tastes, and the body cognizes tactile sensations; thus, amidst these defiled attachments, they amuse themselves and find delight in their fondness for such flavors.
Thus it is, Great Strongman!
The flavor of sensual desire contains much ruin. How so, Great Strongman?
"In what ways does lust lead to ruin? O Great Malla!

Suppose a son of noble family, seeking a livelihood through the mastery of crafts—whether by farming, trading, scribing, studying arithmetic, studying calculation, studying seals, studying poetry, studying *rūpa* (art/craft), teaching writing, or responding to royal commissions—is oppressed by cold, oppressed by heat, endures hunger and thirst, and is bitten by mosquitoes, gadflies, flies, and fleas as he seeks wealth."

When that son of good family exerts himself in such a manner, acts in such a way, and practices with such diligence, yet fails to obtain wealth, he becomes sorrowful and dejected; he weeps, beats his breast, and strikes himself, thereby increasing his delusion as he strives in vain without attaining the fruit.
That son of good family acts in this way, performs in this way, and exerts himself in this way; he thereby acquires wealth, and having acquired wealth, he guards it.
Do not let this wealth be seized by the king; do not let it be stolen by thieves; do not let it be consumed by fire; do not let it rot and decay; do not let it incur loss instead of profit.

He guards his wealth, yet it is seized by the king, stolen by thieves, consumed by fire, or rotted away; he fails to obtain interest on his capital, and thus he becomes sorrowful and unhappy, weeping, beating his breast and striking himself, thereby increasing his delusion.
Furthermore, Mahānāman, that which has been cherished and delighted in throughout the long night is now utterly ruined and lost;
this present body is a mass of suffering caused by lust, arising from lust up to excessive lust—lust is its causal condition.

O Great Malla! Because of lust, and due to the cause of lust reaching its height, mother quarrels with son, son quarrels with mother; father quarrels with son, son quarrels with father; elder brother quarrels with younger sister, younger sister quarrels with elder brother. They fight and dispute; the mother speaks ill of the son, the son speaks ill of the mother; the father speaks ill of the son, the son speaks ill of the father; the elder brother speaks ill of the younger sister, the younger sister speaks ill of the elder brother—how much more so between ordinary people?
"O Great Malla! This present mass of suffering arises because of sensual desire, up to and including excessive sensual desire. O Great Malla!"

It is because of lust, and due to excessive lust, that kings quarrel with kings, brahmins quarrel with brahmins, householders quarrel with householders, thieves quarrel with thieves, and craftsmen quarrel with craftsmen; they each engage in mutual strife and create various weapons of war—whether with fists, stones, or swords and staves—and therein some die or suffer the pains of death. This, Great Strongman, is the case.
"This present mass of suffering arises because of lust, up to and including excessive lust. Great Strongman!

Because of lust, up to and including excessive lust, sentient beings don armor, take up bows and arrows, or don leather armor and carry extremely sharp swords, surrounding one another in gathered combat."

Therein, they may engage in elephant duels, or horse duels, or chariot duels, or infantry duels, or contests with women, or contests with men; therein, some die, which constitutes suffering through death. This, O Great Malla!
"O Great Malla! It is because of lust, up to excessive lust, that this mass of suffering manifests.

Because of lust, up to excessive lust, sentient beings don armor, take up bows and arrows, put on leather cuirasses, and carry extremely sharp swords as they go to a very high city, desiring to attack it."

Within that place, they may blow conch shells, beat drums, or raise their voices in cries; or they may use iron mallets, battle-axes, halberds, sharp wheels, or shoot arrows at one another; or they may hurl down stones in confusion, or use crossbows, or pour molten copper upon them. To die there is suffering—this, Great Strongman, is what it is like.
Now, this present mass of suffering arises because of lust, up to and including excessive lust. O Great Malla!

Because of lust, up to and including excessive lust, sentient beings go to royal cities and towns; they break through walls or open treasuries, steal the property of others, or block the paths of others; they destroy cities, plunder villages, and kill other people.
The officials there seize him and compel him to perform various ascetic penances;
they may cut off his hands, or cut off his feet, or cut off both his hands and feet; or they may cut off his ears, or cut off his nose, or cut off his tongue;
or they may cut off his topknot, or cut off his hair, or cut off both his topknot and his hair; or they may place him inside a wooden chest.

...or they are slaughtered while clothed; or they are placed upon sand and stones, or upon grass, or within the mouths of iron donkeys, or within the mouths of iron lions, or inside copper cauldrons, or inside iron cauldrons;
or they are cut into pieces, or their hands are pierced with sharp forks, or they are laid upon hot iron beds; or else...
Sprinkle them with hot oil, place them in a mortar and pound them with an iron pestle; or use dragon-slime, or strike them with clubs,
or beat them with sticks until they reach the foot of the stake, where their heads are severed with a sword— this, O Great Strongman, is what it means.
"By reason of lust, up to and including excessive lust, this great strongman!

Beings, by reason of lust, up to and including excessive lust, perform bodily austerities, verbal austerities, and mental austerities. At that time, if they fall ill and lie suffering upon their beds, or lie in the shade, with their bodies in extreme and agonizing pain, they find no joy and desire to end their lives."

That is to say, regarding those who practice austerities of body, speech, and mind, at the time of their death they hang upside down, just as when the sun is about to set in the darkness between great mountains and mountain ranges, the shadows of those mountains hang upside down.
Thus it is said: When that person’s life ends while suspended upside down, they reflect:

"By these ascetic practices of body, speech, and mind, while suspended upside down, I have fundamentally failed to perform right conduct or cultivate merit. I have committed many evils—namely, I have pursued evil, acted with greed, and been violent; I have not performed meritorious deeds, nor virtuous deeds, nor anything leading to a higher rebirth. I shall surely fall into that destiny."
"This will lead to regret.
Once regret has arisen, it is unwholesome both at the end and at the beginning. Thus, O Great Strongman!
This mass of suffering in the present life arises because of sensual desire, up to and including excessive sensual desire."

"O Great Malla! Because of lust, and due to excessive lust, sentient beings perform bodily austerities and verbal and mental austerities. Having performed those bodily, verbal, and mental austerities, at the breaking up of the body after death, they are reborn in an evil destination, in hell, on account of that cause and condition."
This is it, Great Strongman!
This is the mass of suffering of the final body, which arises because of lust and reaches its culmination through excessive lust.
This is it, Great Strongman!
The five flavors of sensual pleasure are full of suffering and subject to decay.
This noble disciple,
seeing this as it truly is with equal wisdom, does not delight in sensual pleasures— which are evil and unwholesome dharmas— but instead finds joy in what is called unsurpassed tranquility.
"In this way, Great Malla,
a noble disciple is associated with the dharma of sexual misconduct.
Furthermore, Great Malla..."

I have little craving for sensual pleasure; I know it is suffering, I know it is subject to decay—I know and see this as it truly is—and thus I do not engage in evil or unwholesome states regarding sensual pleasure, but abide in restraint and well-being, which is called unsurpassed peace.
"In this way, Great Strongman!
I am not associated with the dharma of lust.
This, Great Strongman!"
At one time, I was staying at Rājagṛha in the Saptaparṇa Cave, reclining on my right side. Great Malla!

Rising from my afternoon rest, I went to the edge of where I was reclining on my right side; from there, I saw from afar those Nirgranthas who never sit down but remain constantly in a kneeling posture, practicing extreme asceticism.
I went to that place, and having arrived, I spoke these words:
"For what reason, O Nirgrantha?..."
"Why do you practice such constant kneeling and never sitting, performing such extreme asceticism?
He replied to me, saying: "Gautama!..."
There is a teacher, a Nirgrantha who is a kinsman’s son, who speaks thus:
"O you Nirgranthas! You formerly committed evil deeds;

now, by performing these ascetic practices, you shall eliminate those evil deeds. That is to say, whatever evil there may be in the actions of this present body—whether of deed, speech, or mind—you shall not commit it."
I said to them: "How is it, you Nigaṇṭhas! Can your teacher, the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta, truly believe in and abide by that?"
"Do you not doubt that teacher?
He replied: "O Gautama! [I do not. "
"I am a kinsman of that teacher, the Nirgrantha; I have no doubt that I can believe in and abide by his teaching. I replied to him: "It is so."
"O Nirgranthas, just as you are!

There are Nirgranthas who, having previously committed evil deeds and performed extreme ascetic practices, after their death will come to be born among humans; they too shall again train within this Nirgrantha fold, remaining constantly in a kneeling posture and not sitting, performing such ascetic practices."
"Now, all of you in this assembly shall likewise become so. They spoke thus:
"O Gautama! [This is so!]"
"One does not obtain a good retribution from unwholesome conduct; that King Bimbisāra dwells in peace and happiness, whereas you, Śramaṇa Gautama, cannot do so. "O you Nirgranthas!"
It is not that you are at fault for speaking these words. Why is this?
It is because you are an ordinary, foolish person—undisciplined, unwholesome, insatiable, and lacking contentment—who speaks such words.
“King Bimbisāra! He who dwells constantly in the wholesome always attains peace and happiness; the śramaṇa Gautama cannot do so.
Thus you say, O Nirgranthas!
"You should first clarify for me how it is that you claim to dwell in constant peace and happiness,
yet speak of King Bimbisāra and the śramaṇa Gautama?
You, all you Nirgranthas!"
I shall explain this for you.
It is not for the sake of King Bimbisāra of Magadha that I abide in such well-established peace and happiness;
rather, it is for you! You should speak these words:
“King Bimbisāra of Magadha always dwells in constant peace and happiness; this is beyond the reach of you, the śramaṇa Gautama.
“This śramaṇa Gautama! [said the other].
I now ask you: who dwells in well-being and happiness—
the King of Magadha, Bimbisāra, or [the other]?
"Is he a śramaṇa Gautama? [The King asked. "What do you think, Nigaṇṭha?
Does that King Bimbisāra of Magadha possess mastery over his speech and mind?"
"Did you obtain physical well-being and tranquility for seven days and seven nights?
"No, indeed, Gautama!"
"Is it possible, after six, five, four, three, two, or even one day and night, to attain mastery over mind and speech?
And does the body dwell in constant peace and happiness? "Indeed, Gautama!"
"No. "What do you think, Nigaṇṭha?
Do I possess mastery over the faculty of speech?"
“Did you dwell in physical well-being and happiness for one day and one night? “Indeed, Gautama.
“And for two, three, up to seven days and seven nights, were you able to attain mastery over your mind and speech?”
"Are you dwelling in constant peace and happiness?
"Indeed, Gautama. "What do you think, Nigaṇṭha?"
"Among us, who dwells in constant, perfect peace and happiness?
Is it King Bimbisāra of Magadha, or am I?"
"According to the meaning you have understood from what the śramaṇa Gautama has said, the śramaṇa Gautama dwells in well-being and happiness, whereas King Bimbisāra of Magadha does not."
"O Great Malla! There is little flavor in sensual pleasure, but much suffering; within this decay, there is much further decay.

That is to say, O Noble Disciple, one cannot, through wisdom, see things as they truly are, yet commits evil and unwholesome acts regarding sensual pleasure, and does not enter into the unsurpassed peace of joy and bliss."
In this way, Great Strongman!
A noble disciple is associated with the dharma of sensual desire.
Furthermore, Great Strongman!

I have little relish for sensual pleasure and much suffering; knowing this to be subject to decay, I perceive it with wisdom as it truly is. Furthermore, I do not harbor unwholesome states regarding sensual pleasure, but abide in restraint for my own sake, which I call unsurpassed peace.
"In this way, O Great Strongman!
I do not associate with the dharma of lust.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
The Mallas and the bhikṣus, having heard what the Blessed One had spoken, rejoiced and were delighted.
The Sūtra on the Causes of the Aggregate of Suffering Spoken by the Buddha.
